rewrites.blindSummary:
In a city in this state/province on 20 October 2025, a rubbish container was set alight against the façade of a queer cultural centre during the local pride week; the fire was out in about fifteen minutes and nobody was hurt, but security-police investigators took over the arson investigation and a political motive cannot be excluded — local initiatives call it an attempted firebombing, and the attack sits among earlier suspected far-right attacks in the city.

The subsequent local pride parade — the 17th edition — ran with a large police presence against two registered far-right counter-demonstrations, one organised by a far-right youth group, and proceeded without major disruption. The local queer community describes itself as unusually watchful: repeated physical pressure on infrastructure, met by a functioning protective response.
rewrites.blindTangential: The counter-mobilisations and the 2026 anti-right framing centre on far-right hostility to pride/queer visibility generally (pride counter-demonstrations, union coalitions) rather than on trans-specific action — but they define the street climate a visibly queer visitor enters in the local area.

rewrites.blindSummary:
A small inquiry in the state/province's elected legislature, with the interior minister's answer (April 2025), records police-registered queer-hostile offences rising from 33 in 2022 to 83 in 2023 and 135 in 2024 — a year-on-year jump of 52 that the minister's reply calls alarming.

The trend must be read with the national police agency's own caveat: its situation report on LGBTQ* security introduced a new reporting category that makes state/province-by-state/province comparison possible but warns that classification changes can inflate registered counts, so rises may partly reflect better recording rather than a sharper danger. The same answer notes a long-standing network of LGBTQ* liaison officers in every police headquarters, governed by a standing framework concept — an institutional response in place while the statistics remain ambiguous.
rewrites.blindTangential: The recorded rise covers queer-hostile crime generally — the reporting category combines hostility to sexual orientation and to gender-related diversity — so the trend is a general negative-climate signal rather than a trans-specific series.
blindSourceSummaries: A small inquiry in the state/province's elected legislature and the interior minister's answer (April 2025): police-registered queer-hostile offences in this state/province rose from 33 (2022) to 83 (2023) and to 135 (2024, +52 year-on-year — described as alarming); notes a long-standing network of LGBTQ* liaison officers in all police headquarters and a framework concept governing them.

The national police agency's situation report on the security of LGBTQ* people, published with the interior ministry: a multi-year rise in police-registered queer-hostile offences and the new national reporting category that makes state/province-by-state/province comparison possible; classification changes can inflate state/province counts, so cross-state/province numbers need caution.

A regional broadcaster reports (21 August 2025): the state/province interior ministry's answer to a small-inquiry question by three opposition MPs recorded 135 queer-hostile offences in 2024, 52 more than the previous year, among them 16 cases of dangerous grievous bodily harm, seven of bodily harm, 13 of property damage and 26 of insult, with many victims not reporting so that a high dark figure is assumed; the interior minister called the development alarming, attributed part of the responsibility to far-right forces, and the ministry counted suspects identified in 46 of the 2024 proceedings and six convictions. This is the media confirmation of the record's police-registered 33 (2022) to 83 (2023) to 135 (2024) series.

A regional broadcaster reports (17 May 2026) from a further interior-minister answer to an opposition small-inquiry question that this state/province's police counted 141 queer-hostile offences in 2025, against 83 in 2023 and 33 in 2022 — a more than fourfold rise within four years that the minister called alarming and only 'the tip of the iceberg' given the high dark figure; the answer cited a January 2026 tram incident in which a male couple was homophobically insulted, threatened and spat on; the article notes the state/province police keep dedicated contact officers for this hate crime and the state/province government promises consistent prosecution. It updates the record's statistics with the 2025 figure of 141 and confirms the state/province's own alarm at the trend.

A media outlet reports (20 June 2025): a trans woman artist filed a legal complaint under the national equality act after a male security officer refused her a search by a female officer during screening at this state/province's main international airport on 23 November 2024 and told her she was 'not a woman'; the airport later apologised by email, said the security service provider had been instructed to investigate, and promised security staff would be trained on dealing with transgender and gender non-conforming travellers. This is a dated, state/province-specific case of transphobic treatment at the state/province's main international airport — the first screening-gate incident evidence for this record.

rewrites.blindSummary:
The anti-discrimination amendment act of 2025 (assented 30 October 2025; part 3 in force 27 July 2026) removed the civil provision making it unlawful to 'offend, insult, humiliate or intimidate' a person in public on the basis of a protected attribute, including gender identity. This state/province is the only jurisdiction in the country that has actively reversed anti-discrimination protection rather than extended it; the government framed the rollback as 'restoring freedom of speech and religion.' For a visitor, public verbal abuse or humiliation directed at gender expression is now deliberately outside this state/province's law while other state/provinces have brought it inside.

National protections continue to apply uniformly: the 1984 national sex-discrimination law covers gender identity in every state/province, and this state/province's hate-crime penalty enhancements for sexual-orientation- and gender-identity-motivated offences (2022 amendment, effective 2023) remain in force. No criminal expression ban, no facility-access ban, and no conversion-practice-specific enforcement issue arises for a short-term visitor beyond the general national framework.

Remote-area context amplifies practical risk: one remote town registers several thousand offences a year against a population of tens of thousands, and trans community infrastructure in this state/province is thin. A single domestic killing of an Indigenous trans woman (October 2024) is recorded for completeness but is one non-patterned incident and does not support a regional violence finding on its own.

Vs the national score of 0.86, this state/province sits 0.09 below: the deliberate legislative removal of the 'offend, insult, humiliate' protection is the strongest negative sub-national signal in the country, even though it is a civil-law rollback rather than a criminal prohibition. Vs another state/province (0.88), where a 2025 anti-vilification act created the country's first criminal offence for public incitement against a trans person, this state/province moved in the opposite direction in the same year.
rewrites.blindTangential: The removed civil provision protects every attribute (race, religion, sexuality, gender identity) — its repeal signals a broad de-protection climate; gender identity is one named attribute rather than the sole target.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: This state/province's high general assault statistics affect all travellers equally; they appear here only as thin-support and infrastructure context, not as a trans-specific mechanism.
blindSourceSummaries: The state/province legislation page for the assented 2025 anti-discrimination amendment act (assented 30 October 2025; part 3 commencing 27 July 2026), which removes the civil prohibition on offending, insulting, humiliating or intimidating a person in public because of a protected attribute, including gender identity.

A national broadcaster, 17 Oct 2025: this state/province's anti-discrimination amendments passed the legislature, framed as restoring free speech and religious freedom — narrowing the vilification provision and letting religious schools prefer staff sharing the same faith; the government had earlier backtracked from scrapping the vilification section. Marks reduced state/province vilification/discipline protections shaping discrimination exposure for visitors.

The state/province's status page documents the timeline behind this record's assessment: male homosexual activity legal since 1 January 1984 with an equal age of consent since 2003; same-sex marriage from nationwide December 2017 (60.6% 'Yes' in a national vote); full adoption rights since 2018; birth-certificate sex-marker change requiring clinical treatment since 2018; and state/province discrimination protections since 2022, with a March 2025 government announcement and July 2025 bill to repeal the vilification ('offend, insult, humiliate or intimidate') provision. It also records that the state/province government banned rainbow pride flags in public hospitals in February 2025, issued a policy directive in December 2025 banning gender-affirming healthcare for minors, and that the state/province's own hate-crime statute does not list sexual orientation or gender identity (national coverage of those motives only since 2025). The page independently corroborates the record's central claim that this state/province is actively reversing, not extending, anti-discrimination protection.

A national broadcaster, 2 March 2025: the governing party confirmed it would repeal the vilification provision a previous administration added to this state/province's anti-discrimination law three years earlier, which made it unlawful to 'offend, insult, humiliate or intimidate' a person because of a characteristic such as race or gender and could trigger action by the state/province anti-discrimination commission; the top government lawyer framed the change as restoring 'freedom of speech and religion', including letting religious schools again hire only co-religionists. The state/province's anti-discrimination commissioner publicly rebuked the move, warning the government may be 'opening the doors for a very dangerous stream of hate speech'. This is the March 2025 announcement that set in motion the rollback this record describes, which the status-page/legislation trail confirms was enacted as the 2025 anti-discrimination amendment act (assented 30 October 2025).

rewrites.blindSummary:
In August 2026 the state/province assembly passed a new Islamic criminal offences bill — including a clause making gender change an offence for persons under the state/province's Islamic jurisdiction — replacing provisions of the state/province's 2019 Islamic criminal code that the country's national court had struck down as outside state/province power. The bill also carries 'protection of modesty' decency offences, backed by whipping (3–6 strokes), fines up to 5,000 in local currency and imprisonment up to three years.

The sequence — invalidation by the national courts, prompt deliberate re-enactment by the state/province assembly — documents institutional determination to criminalise gender transition, not a stray provision. The gender-change offence binds Muslims, including Muslim travellers exposed to Islamic-law proceedings; the official climate it signals reaches all trans visitors.
rewrites.blindTangential: The same 2026 bill's 'protection of modesty' provisions criminalise general moral and decency conduct for Muslims beyond gender transition — broad Islamic-law policing that reaches same-sex conduct and gender presentation as a category, not trans status alone.
blindSourceSummaries: The state/province's newly passed 2026 Islamic criminal offences bill (passed Aug 2026) contains provisions on modesty, gender change, and safeguarding the modesty of private parts, replacing 16 provisions of the state/province's 2019 Islamic criminal code enactment struck down by the national court. A clause mandates that Muslims safeguard the sanctity and modesty of their private parts in accordance with Islamic law. For this record: the state/province's legislative direction explicitly regulates gender-change matters under Islamic criminal law, with enforcement beginning 2026.

A follow-up report confirms the state/province passed strict new decency rules via the 2026 Islamic criminal offences bill (13 Aug 2026), legislating decency, modesty-covering, and gender-change provisions; the enactment replaces 16 provisions of the 2019 enactment struck down by the national court. The article also notes a related February 2026 first Islamic-court case involving gender change. For this record: confirms the new decency/gender-change legislation is now in force and being applied by the Islamic courts.

rewrites.blindSummary: The most concentrated wave of mob violence against transgender women in the country: ten attacks on 45 victim-survivors in one city between 30 March and 15 July 2026, documented by an advocacy organisation — groups of 10–20 men punched, kicked, threw stones, glass bottles and firecrackers at trans women and stripped some of them naked, filming the assaults for social media. No alleged perpetrator has been publicly identified, arrested or prosecuted; a trans-rights activist who accompanied women filing police reports said officers 'accepted the case but worked on it half-heartedly,' and some survivors were too afraid to report. Separately, on 22 June 2025 police detained 75 people at a villa raid in one district of the same city at a gathering labelled a 'gay party' that violated no law — a rights organisation demanded their release. Activists attribute the violence's legitimisation to a 2025 presidential regulation which from October 2025 lists 'LGBTQ culture' as a national-resilience threat alongside terrorism and drug abuse: people feel able to commit violence arbitrarily because they believe the authorities have legitimised that violence. The pattern-plus-impunity combination is specific to this state/province; national same-sex criminalisation does not by itself explain the street-vigilante wave with total official inaction and explicit anti-trans branding over four months.
rewrites.blindTangential: The 22 June 2025 villa mass detention (75 people) targeted a gay gathering rather than gender identity — same-sex-conduct policing that nonetheless shows the local security apparatus actively mass-proceeds against LGBT people as a category.
blindSourceSummaries: A national broadcaster (15 Aug 2026): men doused a trans woman with what looked like urine on a street in one city in this state/province, one of a wave of attacks; activists link the violence to a 2025 presidential regulation classifying the 'spread of LGBTQ culture' as a non-military threat plus discriminatory regional regulations, saying the authorities' language legitimises violence against trans women. A trans woman quoted says those who previously appeared in public now live in fear. For this record: documents street violence against trans women within the state/province and the national regulatory backdrop enabling it.

For this record: international framing of the raid as unlawful, reinforcing that LGBTI gatherings in the state/province face police action despite violating no law.

rewrites.blindSummary:
The clearest enacted modern local anti-LGBT bylaw in the country: a city's 2024 regional regulation on public order, articles 43-44, prescribes oral and written warnings, cessation of activities, social rehabilitation programmes, and administrative fines of one million in local currency targeting LGBT people. Enforcement is real but contested: a 2026 field study of the regulation's implementation reports supervision, enforcement and guidance by the local order force, with sanctions of suboptimal effectiveness and rehabilitation hampered because the facilities barely exist; a 2025 study records people swept up in LGBT sweeps/apprehensions jumping from 56 in 2023 to 272 in 2024, and customary-law actors pushing parallel measures (a boarding-house barcode system, proposed village regulations on social deviance). A neighbouring regency finalised a draft regulation on public tranquility containing an explicit LGBT prohibition with administrative fines in the tens of millions in local currency plus mandated 'rehabilitation' (psychosocial counselling, spiritual guidance, resocialisation) for people of same-sex attraction. A rights organisation's mapping of discriminatory regional regulations covers eight other state/provinces (not this one, whose key bylaws postdate the study), but documents the same regional-autonomy mechanism this state/province's bylaws instantiate.

This sits below the national score because an enacted bylaw with specified sanctions creates visitor-facing risk (detention, forced rehabilitation programmes, fines) that does not exist in most state/provinces; the documented apprehension counts show the bylaw environment is actively policed, though no caning (a penalty specific to one other state/province) or prosecution under these provisions is recorded. It remains above another state/province (0.06), where patterned mob violence with zero accountability is the primary threat, and above the national floor where no such bylaw exists at all.
rewrites.blindTangential: The enacted city bylaw and the neighbouring regency's draft target LGBT people broadly (same-sex conduct framing); the direct trans-specific element is the 'rehabilitation'/gender-normative enforcement layer and local-order-force profiling of gender-nonconforming people.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly: Social rehabilitation programmes, boarding-house barcode registration and village-level customary sanctions operate on residents; visitors are exposed mainly to sweep/apprehension risk.
blindSourceSummaries: An academic article analysing the 2024 regional public-order regulation of a city in this state/province targeting LGBT people, examined from the perspective of the implementation of Islamic governance: the regulation is framed as responding to local religious values and local customs. For this record: documents a 2024 local anti-LGBT public-order regulation in a city in this state/province, showing formal municipal-level restrictions.

A peer-reviewed study (2025) of LGBT cases in a city in this state/province: recorded cases rose from 56 individuals in 2023 to 272 in 2024; a customary-law community acts as an unofficial actor, initiating the customary-law sanction of expulsion, proposing village regulations on social deviance, and implementing barcode monitoring in boarding houses to police LGBT presence. For this record: documents rising surveillance and customary sanctions against LGBT people within a city in this state/province.

A regional news site (13 May 2026): the regional legislature of a neighbouring regency in this state/province finalised a draft anti-LGBT regional regulation within a public-order and tranquility regulation, including administrative fines and rehabilitation for LGBT people; the drafting body's chair stated that stages have reached finalisation. For this record: a 2026 draft state/province-level regulation introducing fines and 'rehabilitation' targeting LGBT people in a regency of this state/province.

A rights organisation's report (cached copy): maps discriminatory national laws and regional regulations across eight other state/provinces of the country — the reference for the country's regional-bylaw mechanism; this state/province's newer city regulation postdates the mapping.
